extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters (especially those assigned to labor and business beats); journalism students and practitioners learning beat reporting
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for city/newspaper reporters on how to gather, write, and present labor and business news: what to cover, how to cultivate sources, how to remain neutral, and how to translate technical material for general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value routine and personal labor items
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal items and routine labor news (apprentices passing union proficiency exams, small shops unionizing, success stories of members attending night school) are good copy and have social/sociological value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personals and short feature paragraphs to connect with readers who know the individuals; these unexciting chronicles 'fill out the picture of labor' and show that labor consists of individuals with human actions, desires, successes, and failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't assume only explosive labor news matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid believing that labor news is dull unless it is explosive; the belief that 'only bad news is good news' is shortsighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek substantial inside-page stories about routine matters (e.g., contract stipulations about apprentices) and present them as newsworthy even if not spectacular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell what labor is doing without propagandizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Report the activities and provisions of labor organizations rather than serving as a labor propagandist; 'He simply tells the paper's readers all the things labor is doing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use few or no adjectives; present facts so readers are free to form their own judgments (e.g., readers can decide 'Those union fellows are on the right track' or not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cynicism about unions and individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not generalize from a few bad examples or assume unions are dominated by greed or avarice; avoid sweeping negative judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize diversity among union actors (some sacrifice, some are corrupt) and report fairly instead of assuming 'They're all like that.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Make neutrality manifest
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only be neutral but make your stories show that neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a complaint is made by one side, show it to the other side and give an opportunity to answer; if the other side refuses, report who refused and their reason. Keep evidence of visits to both union and management so critics cannot say you favored one side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show both sides and document refusals to reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever management says something about the union or vice versa, present the other side's response or state who refused to reply and why.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly record attempts to contact both sides and specify explanations for any refusals to avoid accusations of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be physically present and visible on both sides of a dispute
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an evident presence at C.L.U. Hall, the strike scene, and management offices so no one can claim imbalance in reporting effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let it be known you are visiting both parties; being seen visiting management as well as union chiefs guards independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize color writing in strikes; emphasize straight reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: During strikes emotions run high; color writing can be interpreted as biased and exaggerate impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understate rather than amplify (e.g., if nine persons were battered, say so directly and soberly); 'he underwrites and says it in low rather than loud voice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise with emotional or collective descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid wording that implies a whole crowd acted when only a few did (e.g., 'Cries of "kill him"' can suggest all 1,500 shouted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase descriptions to avoid misleading impressions; specify numbers or clearly attribute statements to particular subgroups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid loaded or prejudicial words; prefer neutral phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'arbitrary', 'dictation', 'pulled' and phrases like 'on the other hand' can convey prejudice or emotional meaning beyond dictionary senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use neutral alternatives (examples from text: replace 'arbitrary order' with 'a direct order'; render 'a resolution for democracy and autonomy' as 'a resolution described by its sponsors as making for democracy and autonomy'; replace 'dictation' with 'orders').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallel syntax to demonstrate neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel construction when presenting rival facts or figures makes the report appear even-handed and reveals no reporter bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example of membership figures presented in parallel form prevents readers from guessing the reporter's sympathies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premeditatedly and protractedly win confidence of labor chiefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Build long-term trust with labor leaders so they will bring you information you can print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a deliberate, ongoing effort requiring time; once achieved it yields plentiful material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plow the beat during quiet as well as strike times
rubrics_metrics.description: Work the labor beat thoroughly even when there is no immediate trouble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular coverage (columns, recurring items) and attention to personals and features ensures a steady flow of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sidestep cynicism
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciously avoid a cynical stance that dismisses legitimate activities or reforms in labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain curiosity and openness to positive or mundane stories that illuminate the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: When news is incandescent, tell it quietly
rubrics_metrics.description: Even very important or sensational labor news should be reported calmly rather than with shouting or hyperbole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understated presentation helps preserve neutrality and prevents emotional misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn how to manage businessmen (business beat social skill)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reporter must learn to handle and converse with businessmen; fear of businessmen undermines coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach interviews intelligently and respectfully; winning their respect makes them treat the reporter as an equal and opens sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know enough about business to explain it interestingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must understand business language and concepts well enough to translate them for general readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use financial reference books (Moody's, Poor's, Dun & Bradstreet), learn company structure, and be prepared to 'translate' items (e.g., explain cumulative preferred dividends in plain terms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and maintain a personal filing cabinet/morgue and cross-index background
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep biographies and background notes on companies, executives, and local businesses for context and richer stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use files to expand short items into half-columns and to produce timely comparisons (annual meetings, past data). Cross-index for quick retrieval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze business stories by main news currents
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify business reporting opportunities by common pegs: sales volume, employment, new business, finances, technology, personalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use those categories to spot newsworthy angles (e.g., higher-priced goods outselling bargains indicates prosperity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversify sources across business sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on a narrow class of contacts (e.g., only factory executives); cultivate stores, banks, realty firms, and other channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A wide variety of 'listening posts' yields more thorough coverage and prevents blind spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use banks as primary sources for economic trends but win their trust first
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks can indicate loan readiness and general business trends but seldom volunteer unfavorable specifics until they trust you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop patience and reliability to secure bank-provided tips and confirmations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use realty offices as news sources and verify with principals
rubrics_metrics.description: Realtors often know about land sales, building ownership changes, and potential factory expansions before formal announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat realtor tips as leads that require confirmation from the companies or people directly concerned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stores to gauge buying habits and community prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: Retailers notice changes in purchasing patterns that indicate broader economic shifts (e.g., patrons trading up to costlier gifts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow up store observations to produce stories on community economic sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know many people; use every excuse to interview
rubrics_metrics.description: Expanding one's network is central to business-beat success: interviewing new managers, hires, and executives builds dossiers and goodwill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small biographical pieces, photographs, and publicizing promotions create contacts who will share future information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three principles to win businessmen's confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) Question and re-question until information is verified; (2) Ask the boss rather than an underling for authoritative information; (3) Make it unmistakable that you keep confidences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these consistently: verify facts repeatedly, go to decision-makers for policy information, and never break promises about off-the-record remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting facts right is fundamental
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy in numbers and arithmetic is essential; errors damage sources' trust and the reporter's reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double- and triple-check arithmetic and figures (example: an error about 'dollar-a-ton coal' ruined a business source's confidence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate technical/financial material into plain English
rubrics_metrics.description: Business and finance copy often needs unpacking for general readers; explanatory expansions justify extra wordage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert jargon into A-B-C language (example given about cumulative preferred dividends) so general readers can follow and thus increase readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat Chamber of Commerce statements as advocacy when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chamber will freely publicize favorable developments but may spin or downplay negative developments; its statements can be propaganda or arguments rather than plain facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present C. of C. claims for what they are and verify unfavorable stories independently (e.g., closures that 'didn't hurt the city' should be checked).
